text: The Legacy of Stanislavsky
A

Who has had the greatest influence on modern acting? Without doubt it was Konstantin Stanislavsky (1863-1938). He was the great director-teacher who co-founded the Moscow Art Theater, staged the premieres of the works of legendary playwright Anton Chekhov, and created a system of acting explained in books that have become essential for modern actors. He was also the inspiration for several famous American acting schools, which have produced nearly all well-known American film actors since the 1950s.

text: B

Stanislavsky himself had been trained in the classical tradition, but would transform its formal techniques and principles entirely. Actors from Ancient Greece through Elizabethan England to 19th-century Europe would master formal portrayals of love, joy, fear, and anger, which were the same for every play and character. The trademark of classical technique was actors using heightened speech paired with portraying characters with larger-than-life movement. But in more modern times, this theater of illusion has lost ground: the curtains and elaborate arches have been replaced by the plain open stage, and Stanislavsky was the visionary who revolutionized acting technique.

text: C

A simplification of Stanislavsky's own innovative system would go like this: for the performance to have meaning, the actor has to identify with his role. He can do this in a variety of ways: by bringing up memories from his past ; by relying on his imagination; or by focusing on the character's own reality and then breaking the action down into specific units. These methods allow the actor to intensely identify with a character, and this helps involve audiences more deeply in the drama.

text: D

For instance, let's consider the performance of actress Laurie Metcalf, who played the character named Mary Tyrone in Long Day's Journey into Night on the London stage. Everything she did could be seen as an application of Stanislavsky's approach. Her every naturalistic gesture and tone suggested deep identification with her role. In this case, her character evidently had what is known as a 'super objective' to disguise a personal secret from her family. The action also seemed to have been broken down into specific units, up until her last moments when she delivered a heartbreaking final speech while clutching the couch for support. It was great acting.

text: E

Different techniques of acting inspired by Stanislavsky have emerged and influenced each other, and all overlap in at least one respect — in a recognition that the actor's inner world has artistic significance. Each approach is likely to continue to influence theater, film and performance art for decades to come. One of the most famous techniques developed in the US is that of Lee Strasberg, who was an actor himself. Lee Strasberg's technique encourages actors to magnify and intensify their connection to the material by creating their characters' emotional experiences in their real lives. He insisted the actor concentrate on his feelings derived from memories of his own experience. However, this method has been criticized for the obvious dangers of a psychological nature that it presents to the performer.

text: F

Stella Adler was the only American actor to study with Stanislavsky himself, and developed her own method built on the work of Stanislavsky and Lee Strasberg. Adler's technique differs from Strasberg's in that it emphasizes imagination over emotional recall. She famously said, 'Drawing on the emotions I experienced to create a role is sick and schizophrenic. If that is acting, I don't want to do it.' Instead, Adler coached actors to imagine their character's life in rich detail and to analyze a script from their character's perspective.

text: G

Sanford Meisner developed his unique approach in the 1930s after working with Lee Strasberg and Stella Adler. Meisner's method is an especially practical one, in which students are frequently told to 'get out of their heads'. His famous practice has two actors sit opposite each other and respond in the moment by echoing a phrase back and forth. Instead of focusing on structured performances, actors were taught how to be more open, flexible, and better listeners.

text: H

Renowned dramatist and Stanislavsky's star student, Michael Chekhov, developed his own acting technique in the United States in the late 1920s. Chekhov pioneered a psycho-physical approach to acting, focusing on a conscious awareness of the immediate sights and sounds even the smell, taste, and texture of the moment. In his technique, a character's needs are first made physical in the form of an external gesture. Subsequently, this gesture is suppressed and incorporated inwardly, allowing the physical memory to influence the performance on an unconscious level.

text: I

The action-based acting technique called Practical Aesthetics was developed by playwright David Mamet and actor William H. Macy, and incorporates elements of Stanislavsky and Meisner as well as ideas of the Greek philosopher Epictetus. The philosopher taught acceptance of circumstances and advocated a calm manner when responding to given events. Practical Aesthetics involves a four-step scene analysis that highlights pursuit of an action; actors are taught to limit their attention to what is literally taking place on stage as well as the objectives of the other players.
